content: Pediculosis pubis, commonly referred to as crabs or pubic lice, is an infestation caused by the parasitic insect Pthirus pubis. This organism primarily inhabits human pubic hair but can also infest other hair-bearing areas, such as the eyelashes, leading to a condition known as pediculosis ciliaris. The hallmark symptom of this infestation is intense itching in the pubic region. Effective treatment typically involves topical agents like permethrin or pyrethrin combined with piperonyl butoxide. Globally, approximately 2% of the population is affected by this condition. Historically, pediculosis pubis was first documented in the medical literature in 1946, with Andrew G. Franks describing the use of DDT as a treatment option at that time. Infestations can be classified based on the affected site: Phthiriasis pubis: Infestation of pubic hair. Phthiriasis palpebrarum: Infestation of eyelashes. Pathophysiology Transmission Pubic lice are most commonly transmitted through intimate physical contact, particularly sexual contact. In some cases, parent-to-child transmission can occur via shared towels, clothing, bedding, or closets. Adults are more frequently affected than children. Pubic lice cannot survive for long outside the warmth and humidity of the human body, typically dying within 24–48 hours without a blood meal. In children, infestation does not necessarily indicate sexual abuse, but this possibility should be considered. Life Cycle The life cycle of Pthirus pubis consists of three stages: egg (nit), nymph, and adult. Eggs (nits): These are laid on hair shafts, with females producing approximately 30 eggs during their 3–4 week lifespan. Eggs hatch after about a week, releasing nymphs. Nymphs: These immature lice resemble smaller versions of adults and undergo three molts before maturing. Adults: Adult lice are tan to grayish-white in color and resemble miniature crabs under magnification. They are broader than head or body lice and require human blood to survive. If removed from the host, they die within 1–2 days. Transmission primarily occurs through sexual contact, though fomites (e.g., bedding, clothing) may play a minor role. Macroscopic Characteristics Pubic lice exist in three forms: Nits (eggs): Oval, yellow to white, and firmly attached to hair shafts. They are often difficult to see. Nymphs: Immature lice that feed on blood and mature into adults within 2–3 weeks. Adults: Resembling crabs, they have six legs, with the front two resembling pincers. Females are larger than males and lay nits. Without a blood meal, adults die within 1–2 days. Causes The causative organism of pubic lice infestation is Pthirus pubis. Differentiating Pediculosis Pubis from Other Diseases Pediculosis pubis must be distinguished from other conditions that cause itching and excoriation in the pubic area. Epidemiology and Demographics The global incidence of pubic lice is estimated at 2,000 cases per 100,000 individuals. However, accurate data is challenging to obtain due to underreporting, as many cases are self-treated or discreetly managed by personal physicians. Recent trends in pubic hair removal may have contributed to a decline in pubic lice populations in some regions. Risk Factors Sexual contact with an infected individual is the primary risk factor for transmission. Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis Natural History If untreated, pubic lice infestation can persist and lead to secondary bacterial infections due to intense scratching. Complications The most common complication is excoriation from scratching, which may result in secondary bacterial infections. When the eyelashes are infested, conditions such as blepharitis and conjunctivitis may occur. Prognosis With appropriate medical treatment, pediculosis pubis has an excellent prognosis. Screening There are no specific screening recommendations for pubic lice. History and Symptoms Pubic lice primarily colonize the genital and peri-anal regions but may also infest abdominal, axillary, beard, and mustache hair in males. In children, they are often found on the eyelashes. The main symptom is itching, caused by hypersensitivity to louse saliva, which typically develops 2 or more weeks after initial infestation. Other findings may include erythematous sores from scratching and characteristic gray-blue discoloration (maculae ceruleae) at feeding sites. Physical Examination A skin examination may reveal: Visualization of lice and nits in the pubic area or other affected sites (e.g., perianal, inguinal, axillary, chest hair, or eyelashes). Papular urticaria. Excoriations, which may become secondarily infected. Maculae ceruleae, a pathognomonic finding for pubic lice, appearing as gray-blue spots scattered over the lower abdomen, buttocks, and upper thighs. Laboratory Findings Diagnosis is made through direct visualization of lice on pubic hair. There are no associated laboratory findings. Other Diagnostic Studies Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying lice on pubic hair. Medical Therapy All patients with pediculosis pubis require antimicrobial therapy. Randomized clinical data comparing the efficacy and safety of treatments are limited, with most studies extrapolated from head lice management. Recommended treatments include: Permethrin 1% cream rinse applied to affected areas and washed off after 10 minutes. Pyrethrin with piperonyl butoxide applied to affected areas and washed off after 10 minutes. Ivermectin (250 µg/kg orally), which may be repeated in 1–2 weeks. Malathion lotion applied to dry hair and washed off after 8–12 hours. Special Considerations Eyelashes: Topical ophthalmic ointments or petroleum jelly should be applied to the eyelid margins twice daily for 10 days. Pregnancy: Permethrin and pyrethrin are preferred treatments. Ivermectin may be used, as no teratogenicity has been observed in humans, but other drugs are generally preferred. Non-Pharmacologic Management Clothing and bedding should be decontaminated by laundering at temperatures above 50°C. Treatment of Sexual Partners All sexual partners within the previous 30 days should be evaluated and treated. Sexual contact should be avoided until all partners have completed treatment and are cured. Patients diagnosed with pubic lice should also be screened for other sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Surgery There is no role for surgery in the treatment of pubic lice. Primary Prevention Abstaining from sexual contact with an infected individual is an effective preventive measure. Secondary Prevention Preventive measures include: Washing and drying all clothing and bedding in hot water. Promoting personal hygiene and sanitation. Treating sexual contacts of individuals with pubic lice. Screening patients and their sexual partners for other STIs.
